Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Vignette:
Mateo was thirty-two when the nights in their shared apartment began to carry a weight he could not quite name, though he would not understand it fully until months later. He had come to believe that the physical abuse had not been a single violent outburst, but a slow, suffocating pressure that began with his partner’s unpredictable movements and escalated until Mateo found himself physically held down against the kitchen door, unable to push free. The sensory details of that period etched themselves into his mind: the sharp crack of the entryway door when his partner turned abruptly, the thick, sweet scent of whiskey that clung to the walls, and the firm, unyielding grip on his upper arms that felt less like an embrace and more like a trap. Now, when he recalls the event, the memories arrive with startling clarity, each detail preserved in sharp relief. More than just recollection, he feels an overwhelming grief wash over him, a quiet sorrow that rises in his chest whenever the past surfaces. Sometimes, the sounds return first—the familiar creak of a hinge or the distant thud of a latch—echoing in his head as if the kitchen door were still swinging shut. In the weeks and months that followed, Mateo’s daily life began to bend around these sensations. He avoided going to the old neighborhood entirely, yet found himself drawn back to its edges, walking the perimeter of the apartment building rather than stepping inside. The parish hall where he worked as a Social Ministry Worker became both a refuge and a mirror of his trauma. When parishioners moved suddenly past his desk, his body reacted as though danger were already upon him, his shoulders hiking up before his mind could catch up. He had learned to brace himself for impact, though he worked tirelessly to keep his face steady, determined to control the emotions that threatened to spill over during counseling sessions and community dinners. The smell of alcohol, whether from a neighbor’s late-night bottle or the wine served at ministry gatherings, would instantly ground him back in that old kitchen, and he would pause, certain that the floor might give way. Nights proved the hardest; while daylight offered a kind of armor, darkness stripped it away, and he remained restless and hyperalert, convinced that any shadowed corner could conceal the same pressure that had once pinned him down. His avoidance habits settled into a quiet routine that gradually reshaped his work and daily rhythm. At the parish hall, Mateo developed a pattern of lingering near the entrance, his eyes tracking every door that opened or slammed shut. He could not remember the last time he had left without pressing his palm against the deadbolt three times, listening for the solid click of the lock. During home visits to families in need, he would sometimes freeze completely when a resident darted toward him or a neighbor reached out, his breath catching until the moment passed. He had come to accept this stillness as necessary, though it often meant he missed the first part of a conversation or delayed responding to a request. His divorce had not been sudden, and the parallel weight of his heightened awareness and his effort to appear composed had worn him thin. Friends noted how he carefully measured his reactions, never shouting, never shrinking, simply holding himself together with a quiet, persistent effort. Now at thirty-seven, Mateo stands at the threshold of seeking formal support, prompted by a recent assignment that required him to stay overnight at the old apartment building. The nights there have become a quiet trial, his vigilance sharpened by the scent of aged wood and the familiar groan of settling floors. He knows that the grief he carries is not a weakness but a testament to what he survived, yet he worries that his careful control may be turning into a kind of isolation. What he hopes for is not the erasure of the past, but a way to move through the world without bracing for every slam of a door, every sudden shift of light, every familiar weight of a hand. He is ready to step fully into the spaces he has skirted for years, trusting that the memories, however vivid and tearful, no longer hold him captive.
